prompt: What does 'system development methodology' refer to in the course text?

options.text: A single diagram showing the data flows of a system
The structured approaches, models and techniques used to plan, analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems
The list of deliverables for the support phase
A software product used to build system components

explanation: A methodology is the whole structured way of developing a system: approaches, models and techniques across every phase.

why.a: Wrong. That describes a DFD, one model among many.
why.b: Correct. That is the text's definition.
why.c: Wrong. Deliverables are outputs of phases, not the methodology.
why.d: Wrong. A software product is a TOOL.

prompt: True or false: the course text says developing information systems without a clear methodology often leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet requirements.
explanation: That is the text's case for having a methodology at all.

why.true: Correct. Those three consequences are named.
why.false: Wrong. The text names exactly these consequences.

prompt: The course text calls a Systems Development Methodology a framework used to do three things to the development of an information system. Which three?
explanation: A methodology is the standard process an organisation follows, a framework to structure, plan and control development.

why.a: Correct. Structure, plan and control.
why.b: Wrong. Those are implementation work, not what a framework does.
why.c: Wrong. Those are fact-finding techniques.
why.d: Wrong. Those are support activities.

prompt: Which two of these are among the five methodologies the course text covers in this unit?
explanation: The five: Waterfall, Rapid Application Development, Prototyping, the Incremental model, and Agile.

why.a: Correct. RAD is one of the five.
why.b: Wrong. JRP is a fact-finding technique, in Module Two.
why.c: Correct. The Incremental model is one of the five.
why.d: Wrong. Functional decomposition is how a system is split into subsystems.

prompt: Which methodology is a traditional, linear approach in which each phase must be completed before the next begins?
explanation: Waterfall proceeds sequentially, like a natural waterfall: each phase complete before the next begins.

why.a: Wrong. Agile is iterative and incremental.
why.b: Wrong. Evolutionary prototyping loops through build and feedback.
why.c: Wrong. RAD is iterative development.
why.d: Correct. Waterfall.

prompt: In Waterfall, to whom are each phase's key deliverables presented for approval before the project moves on?

options.text: The approval committee and the project sponsor

explanation: Deliverables go to the approval committee and project sponsor at the end of each phase. That gate is what makes Waterfall controlled and slow.

why.a: Correct. The approval committee and project sponsor.
why.b: Wrong. Scribe and facilitator are JRP roles.
why.c: Wrong. The help desk belongs to support.
why.d: Wrong. Users sign off too, but the approval named is by the committee and sponsor.

prompt: Strict monitoring in Waterfall is ensured through which two of these?

options.text: Daily face-to-face stand-ups instead of documents
User and IT management sign-off at the end of each phase
Releasing an incomplete system to users early

explanation: Three controls: extensive written documentation, formal reviews, and user and IT management sign-off at the end of each phase.

why.a: Correct. Extensive documentation is one of the controls.
why.b: Wrong. Preferring face-to-face over documentation is Agile.
why.c: Correct. Sign-off at each phase end.
why.d: Wrong. Delivering an incomplete system early is RAD's chief disadvantage, not a Waterfall control.

prompt: What are the two important variants of the Waterfall model in the course text?
explanation: Parallel Development and the V-Model both keep Waterfall's structure: Parallel to save time, V to build testing in.

why.a: Wrong. Those are the two types of PROTOTYPING.
why.b: Wrong. Those are Agile methods.
why.c: Correct. Parallel Development and the V-Model.
why.d: Wrong. Spiral is adaptive and Incremental is its own methodology.

prompt: Which two of these are advantages of Waterfall in the course text?

options.text: It provides structure to inexperienced staff
The customer can preview the system early

explanation: The four advantages: easy to understand and use; structure for inexperienced staff; documentation and reviews give quality, reliability and maintainability; progress is measurable.

why.a: Correct. Structure for inexperienced staff.
why.b: Wrong. Difficulty responding to change is a DISADVANTAGE of Waterfall.
why.c: Correct. Measurable progress.
why.d: Wrong. Little opportunity to preview is a DISADVANTAGE.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of Waterfall's disadvantages in the course text?

options.text: Forward-only progress gives a false impression of progress
Problems are often not discovered until system testing
It produces excessive documentation that is time-consuming to update
It provides no structure for inexperienced staff

explanation: The reverse is an ADVANTAGE: Waterfall provides structure to inexperienced staff. The six disadvantages: inflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome; false impression of progress; little chance to preview; problems found late; hard to change; excessive documentation.

why.a: Wrong choice, because this IS a disadvantage.
why.b: Wrong choice, because this IS a disadvantage.
why.c: Wrong choice, because this IS a disadvantage.
why.d: Correct. Waterfall's structure for inexperienced staff is one of its advantages.

prompt: True or false: one disadvantage of Waterfall is that there is little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late.
explanation: The customer sees the system only near the end, so problems found then are expensive.

why.true: Correct. That is one of the six disadvantages.
why.false: Wrong. It is listed among the disadvantages.

prompt: True or false: the course text says Waterfall is used when there is strong pressure for immediate implementation.
explanation: Waterfall is used when there is NO pressure for immediate implementation, along with clear objectives, stable and comprehensive requirements, and a large, expensive, complicated project.

why.true: Wrong. The text says no pressure for immediate implementation.
why.false: Correct. Waterfall is slow; it suits projects with no rush.

prompt: Which two kinds of project does the course text say Waterfall is best suited for?
explanation: Stable, well-understood requirements: government systems, financial applications, and regulatory or safety-critical systems.

why.a: Correct. Government systems are named.
why.b: Wrong. Short-lived demonstrations are a use of evolutionary prototyping.
why.c: Correct. Regulatory or safety-critical systems are named.
why.d: Wrong. Unstable requirements are exactly what Waterfall handles badly.

prompt: Why was the Parallel Model designed, according to the course text?

options.text: To remove the need for analysis
To reduce the long development time of strictly sequential phases
To add risk analysis to Waterfall
To let users work with an incomplete system

explanation: It keeps Waterfall's structured, predictive nature but runs some activities at the same time, to cut the long sequential development time.

why.a: Wrong. General analysis still comes first.
why.b: Correct. To reduce the long development time.
why.c: Wrong. Lack of risk analysis is a V-model weakness; the Parallel model is not described as fixing it.
why.d: Wrong. That is the chief disadvantage of iterative development.

prompt: In the Parallel Model, WHEN is the system divided into subprojects?

options.text: After the general analysis and high-level design phases are completed
Only after the support phase begins

explanation: General analysis and high-level design first; then subprojects each run detailed design, implementation and testing at the same time, and are finally integrated into one system.

why.a: Wrong. The general analysis must be done first.
why.b: Correct. After general analysis and high-level design.
why.c: Wrong. By then there is nothing left to run in parallel.
why.d: Wrong. Support is after the system is built.

prompt: True or false: in the Parallel Model, once all the subprojects are complete they are integrated into a single system.
explanation: The subprojects run detailed design, implementation and testing side by side, then come together as one system.

why.true: Correct. Integration into one system is the final step.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: True or false: in the V-Shape Model, testing activities proceed DOWN the left side of the V and development activities move UP the right side.
explanation: The other way round: development goes down the left, testing comes up the right, each development phase paired with its testing phase.

why.true: Wrong. Development is down the left; testing is up the right.
why.false: Correct. The sides are the other way round.

prompt: Which two of these are advantages of the V-Shaped Model in the course text?

options.text: It improves overall quality through early development of test plans
It handles dynamic changes in requirements easily
Verification and validation are done early in development
It contains thorough risk analysis activities

explanation: Five advantages: simple; better quality through early test plans; milestones to track progress; high-quality deliverables; verification and validation early.

why.a: Correct. Early test plans improve quality.
why.b: Wrong. Not handling dynamic change easily is a DISADVANTAGE.
why.c: Correct. Early verification and validation.
why.d: Wrong. The text says it does NOT contain risk analysis activities.

prompt: Which of these is a DISADVANTAGE of the V-Shaped Model in the course text?

options.text: It does not contain risk analysis activities
Test plans are developed too early
Progress cannot be tracked by milestones

explanation: The four disadvantages: the rigidity of waterfall; not easily handling dynamic changes; not suiting a dynamic business environment; no risk analysis activities.

why.a: Correct. No risk analysis is one of the four.
why.b: Wrong. Early test plans are an ADVANTAGE.
why.c: Wrong. Tracking by milestones is an ADVANTAGE.
why.d: Wrong. Simple and straightforward is an ADVANTAGE.

prompt: Which example does the course text give of a system for which the V-Shaped Model is used?
explanation: The V model is used when high reliability is needed, such as hospital patient control, when all requirements are known up front, and when the solution and technology are known.

why.a: Wrong. Short-lived demonstrations suit evolutionary prototyping.
why.b: Correct. Hospital patient control, a high-reliability system.
why.c: Wrong. Games are the text's example of merely IMPORTANT, not critical, reliability.
why.d: Wrong. Prototype interfaces suit evolutionary prototyping.

prompt: True or false: the V-Shaped Model is used when all requirements are known up front and the solution and technology to be used are known.
explanation: Known requirements, known solution and technology, and a need for high reliability: the V model's three conditions.

why.true: Correct. Both conditions are in the text.
why.false: Wrong. The text lists both conditions.

prompt: What other name does the course text give Rapid Application Development?
explanation: RAD is also called iterative development: special techniques and tools speed up analysis, design and implementation so a portion of the system reaches users quickly for feedback.

why.a: Correct. Iterative development.
why.b: Wrong. Throwaway prototyping is also called rapid or EXPLORATORY prototyping, not RAD.
why.c: Wrong. Parallel development is a Waterfall variant.
why.d: Wrong. Not a name the text gives RAD.

prompt: True or false: RAD reduces project risk by breaking the project into smaller segments, and aims at a high-quality system at relatively low investment cost.
explanation: RAD emphasises quick delivery through reusable components, visual tools and intensive user involvement, in smaller segments that reduce risk.

why.true: Correct. Both statements are in the text.

prompt: Which two of these are RAD tools in the course text?
explanation: RAD tools: GUI builders, CASE tools, DBMSs, fourth-generation languages, code generators, object-oriented techniques.

why.a: Correct. GUI builders are RAD tools.
why.b: Wrong. Questionnaires are a fact-finding technique.
why.c: Correct. Code generators are RAD tools.
why.d: Wrong. Decision tables document business rules.

prompt: Which two of these are RAD ADVANTAGES in the course text?

options.text: The time-box approach mitigates cost and schedule risk
There is a risk of never achieving closure
Focus moves from documentation to code, described as WYSIWYG
Users begin with a system that is intentionally incomplete

explanation: Advantages: documentation to code (WYSIWYG); effective user feedback; time-boxing mitigates cost and schedule risk; lower cost; new requirements fed into later versions. Never achieving closure and the incomplete system are disadvantages.

why.a: Correct. Time-boxing is an advantage.
why.b: Wrong. Never achieving closure is a DISADVANTAGE.
why.c: Correct. WYSIWYG, documentation to code.
why.d: Wrong. The intentionally incomplete system is the CHIEF disadvantage.

prompt: What does the course text call the CHIEF disadvantage of iterative development?

options.text: Users begin to work with a system that is intentionally incomplete

explanation: Users receive a partial system on purpose, and must work with what is not yet there.

why.a: Wrong. Excessive documentation is a Waterfall disadvantage.
why.b: Correct. The intentionally incomplete system.
why.c: Wrong. No risk analysis is a V-model disadvantage.
why.d: Wrong. Slow and cumbersome is Waterfall.

prompt: True or false: one RAD disadvantage is that user expectations may increase and requirements expand, leading to scope creep.
explanation: Rapid delivery makes users ask for more, which expands scope. Along with the risk of never achieving closure.

why.false: Wrong. It is one of the five disadvantages.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the conditions under which the course text says RAD is used?

options.text: The user will be involved throughout the life cycle

explanation: RAD is used when requirements are reasonably well known, users are involved throughout, technical risks are low, high performance is NOT required, and functionality comes in increments.

why.a: Wrong choice, because this IS a condition for RAD.
why.b: Wrong choice, because this IS a condition for RAD.
why.c: Correct. The text says RAD is used when high performance is NOT required.
why.d: Wrong choice, because this IS a condition for RAD.

prompt: Which methodology combines linear and iterative approaches and sits between Waterfall and prototyping?
explanation: The Incremental model builds the system in increments, each adding functionality on top of the last, mixing linear and iterative.

why.a: Wrong. The V model is a linear Waterfall variant.
why.b: Wrong. Agile is adaptive, iterative and incremental, not described as between Waterfall and prototyping.
why.c: Correct. The Incremental model.
why.d: Wrong. Throwaway prototyping discards its prototypes.

prompt: True or false: in the Incremental model, changes to the CURRENT increment can be accepted at any time during its development.
explanation: Further requirements analysis can be done for LATER increments, but changes for the current increment cannot be accepted.

why.true: Wrong. The text says changes for the current increment cannot be accepted.
why.false: Correct. Only later increments can take new requirements.

prompt: In the Incremental model, what happens to the services customers outline?

options.text: They are all built at once in a single release
They are prioritised and grouped into increments, and the first increment is defined in detail and developed
They are thrown away after a prototype
They are left until the support phase

explanation: Prioritise, group into increments, develop the first in detail, integrate later increments with the existing ones.

why.a: Wrong. That would be Waterfall's single delivery.
why.b: Correct. Prioritised and grouped into increments.
why.c: Wrong. Discarding is throwaway prototyping.
why.d: Wrong. Increments are built during development.

prompt: Which two of these are advantages of the Incremental model in the course text?

options.text: High-risk or major functions are developed first
It needs no planning or design
Each release delivers an operational product

explanation: Seven advantages, including: high-risk functions first; each release operational; lower initial cost; divide and conquer; faster first delivery; important functionality early; reduced risk.

why.a: Correct. High-risk functions first.
why.b: Wrong. The text lists the need for good planning and design as a DISADVANTAGE.
why.c: Correct. Each release is operational.
why.d: Wrong. The need for well-defined module interfaces is a DISADVANTAGE.

prompt: Which of these is a DISADVANTAGE of the Incremental model in the course text?

options.text: Difficulty mapping customer requirements to increments of the right size

explanation: Five disadvantages: sizing increments; finding common facilities; needing good planning and design; needing an early complete definition; needing well-defined interfaces. The other options are advantages.

why.a: Wrong. Early functionality is an ADVANTAGE.
why.b: Correct. Sizing increments is hard.
why.c: Wrong. Lower initial cost is an ADVANTAGE.
why.d: Wrong. Faster first delivery is an ADVANTAGE.

prompt: How does the course text describe the first version built in prototyping?

options.text: A quick and dirty version with minimal features

explanation: Quick and dirty, minimal features; it is reanalysed, redesigned and reimplemented after user reactions until analysts, users and sponsor agree it has enough functionality.

why.a: Wrong. The first prototype is deliberately minimal.
why.b: Correct. Quick and dirty, minimal features.
why.c: Wrong. That is a document, not a prototype.
why.d: Wrong. That is a UML diagram.

prompt: Match each prototyping term with its description in the course text.

pairs.right: A temporary prototype built quickly and discarded once requirements are clear
An initial version refined and expanded until it becomes the final system
Build early for feedback; repeat until users, analysts and sponsor agree

explanation: Two types: THROWAWAY (also rapid or exploratory) discards its prototype and builds the real system with a structured method; EVOLUTIONARY keeps refining until the prototype IS the system.

prompt: In evolutionary prototyping, which requirements does development START with?

options.text: The requirements that are least understood
The requirements that are best understood
The requirements with the most technical risk
The requirements of the support phase

explanation: Evolutionary prototyping aims to deliver a working system, so it starts with what is best understood. Throwaway prototyping is the one that explores the poorly understood, risky parts.

why.a: Wrong. Exploring the unclear is what THROWAWAY prototypes are for.
why.b: Correct. It starts with the best-understood requirements.
why.c: Wrong. Design prototypes of high-risk areas belong to throwaway prototyping.
why.d: Wrong. Not a starting point in the text.

prompt: True or false: in evolutionary prototyping the designer builds the database, user interface and algorithmic functions, demonstrates the prototype, and the user suggests improvements, looping until the user is satisfied.
explanation: Build, demonstrate, evaluate, improve, repeat, until the prototype becomes the final system.

why.true: Correct. That is the evolutionary loop.
why.false: Wrong. The text describes exactly this loop.

prompt: Which two of these are advantages of evolutionary prototyping?

options.text: Customers can SEE requirements as they are gathered

explanation: Advantages: customers see requirements; a more accurate product; unexpected requirements accommodated; developers learn from customers; flexible design; interaction stimulates awareness of more needs.

why.a: Correct. Seeing requirements as they are gathered.
why.b: Wrong. The text warns the process may continue forever.
why.c: Correct. Unexpected requirements can be accommodated.
why.d: Wrong. The text warns maintainability may be overlooked.

prompt: Which of these is a DISADVANTAGE of evolutionary prototyping in the course text?

options.text: Customers can see requirements as they are gathered
A tendency to abandon structured program development for code-and-fix

explanation: Disadvantages: code-and-fix; little methodical analysis; a quick-and-dirty reputation; maintainability overlooked; the customer may want the prototype delivered; it may continue forever (scope creep).

why.a: Wrong. That is an ADVANTAGE.
why.b: Wrong. That is an ADVANTAGE.
why.c: Correct. Code-and-fix is a disadvantage.
why.d: Wrong. That is an ADVANTAGE.

prompt: The course text lists when evolutionary prototyping is used. Which two of these are on that list?

options.text: When requirements are fully stable and documented

explanation: Used when requirements are unstable or need clarifying, as the clarification stage of a waterfall, for user interfaces, short-lived demonstrations, new original development, and the analysis and design parts of object-oriented development.

why.a: Correct. User interfaces are on the list.
why.b: Wrong. High-reliability hospital systems are the V model's example.
why.c: Correct. Short-lived demonstrations are on the list.
why.d: Wrong. Stable requirements suit Waterfall.

prompt: True or false: in throwaway prototyping the prototype becomes the final operational system.
explanation: Throwaway prototypes are DISCARDED once requirements are clarified, and the real system is built with a more structured methodology. Becoming the final system is evolutionary prototyping.

why.false: Correct. The throwaway prototype is discarded.

prompt: What does throwaway prototyping do BEFORE its design prototypes are built?

options.text: It has a thorough analysis phase to gather requirements

explanation: Thorough analysis first; then design prototypes for the parts not fully understood or technically risky. That combination is why it produces stable, reliable systems.

why.a: Wrong. Installation is near the end.
why.b: Correct. A thorough analysis phase comes first.
why.c: Wrong. Throwaway prototyping is known for thorough analysis.
why.d: Wrong. Increments belong to the Incremental model.

prompt: True or false: the course text says evolutionary prototyping risks weak architecture and difficult documentation.
explanation: Evolutionary prototyping suits evolving requirements and rapid delivery, at the risk of weak architecture and hard documentation. Throwaway prototyping suits unclear requirements.

why.true: Correct. Those are the risks named.
why.false: Wrong. The text names both risks.

prompt: According to the course text, what is special about each iteration in the Agile model?

options.text: Every iteration is a complete software project
Every iteration is approved by an approval committee

explanation: Agile is adaptive, iterative and incremental; each iteration is a complete project, documentation overhead is cut, and face-to-face communication is preferred.

why.a: Correct. Each iteration is a complete software project.
why.b: Wrong. Committee approval is Waterfall.
why.c: Wrong. Agile eliminates documentation overhead.
why.d: Wrong. Discarding is throwaway prototyping.

prompt: True or false: in Agile, face-to-face communication is preferred over modelling and documentation.
explanation: Modelling and documentation overhead is eliminated; people talk instead.

why.true: Correct. The text says face-to-face communication is preferred.
why.false: Wrong. The text says exactly this.

prompt: What is delivered at the end of each Agile sprint?

options.text: A working increment, for user evaluation and feedback

explanation: Each short, time-boxed sprint includes requirement analysis, design, coding, testing and review, and ends with a working increment.

why.a: Wrong. Agile favours working software over documents.
why.b: Correct. A working increment.
why.c: Wrong. Agile increments are kept, not thrown away.
why.d: Wrong. Every sprint delivers something working.

prompt: Which two of these are Agile activities in the course text?

options.text: Creation and prioritisation of user stories
Formal sign-off by an approval committee

explanation: Agile activities: user stories created and prioritised, sprint planning and task assignment, development and testing within each sprint, sprint review and retrospective.

why.a: Correct. User stories are created and prioritised.
why.b: Wrong. Committee sign-off is Waterfall.
why.c: Correct. Sprint review and retrospective.
why.d: Wrong. Parallel conversion is an installation approach.

prompt: Which two of these are popular Agile methods named in the course text?
explanation: The Agile methods: Crystal Clear, Scrum, Extreme Programming, Lean Software Development, Kanban.

why.a: Correct. Scrum is one of the five named Agile methods.
why.b: Wrong. Gane-Sarson is a DFD notation.
why.c: Correct. Extreme Programming is one of the five.
why.d: Wrong. The V-Model is a Waterfall variant.

prompt: True or false: the course text says one methodology is always best, so the choice is simple.
explanation: Selecting the methodology is the project manager's first challenge, and it is not simple because no one methodology is always best.

why.true: Wrong. The text says no one methodology is always best.
why.false: Correct. The choice is not simple.

prompt: Which two of these are among the six methodology selection criteria?

options.text: The colour of the user interface

explanation: The six criteria: clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, schedule visibility.

why.a: Correct. Clarity of requirements.
why.b: Wrong. Not a criterion.
why.c: Correct. Schedule visibility.
why.d: Wrong. Not a criterion.

prompt: Match each selection criterion with the methodology the course text recommends for it.

pairs.right: Throwaway prototyping, with design prototypes of high-risk areas
Throwaway prototyping, but NOT system prototyping
RAD, iterative development and system prototyping
RAD, which moves critical design decisions earlier

explanation: The table the whole of test 1 leaned on. Throwaway prototyping appears four times: unclear requirements, unfamiliar technology, complexity and reliability. RAD owns short schedules and schedule visibility.

prompt: For a COMPLEX system, which approach does the course text say is NOT well suited?

options.text: Careful and detailed analysis and design

explanation: Complex systems need careful, detailed analysis and design. Throwaway prototyping provides that; system prototyping does not.

why.a: Wrong. Throwaway prototyping IS well suited to complex systems.
why.b: Correct. The text says system prototyping is NOT suited to complex systems.
why.c: Wrong. That is exactly what complex systems need.
why.d: Wrong. The text does not name the V-model as unsuitable here.

prompt: A project must be delivered by a fixed, close date. Which methodologies does the course text recommend?

options.text: RAD methodologies, iterative development and system prototyping

explanation: RAD accelerates development, and iterative development and system prototyping let the team adjust functionality to meet a specific delivery date.

why.a: Wrong. Both are slow, sequential approaches.
why.b: Correct. RAD, iterative development and system prototyping.
why.c: Wrong. Throwaway is recommended for unclear requirements, unfamiliar technology, complexity and reliability.
why.d: Wrong. Not the text's recommendation for short schedules.

prompt: True or false: for schedule visibility, the course text recommends RAD because it moves many critical design decisions earlier in the project.
explanation: Earlier decisions let managers recognise and address risk factors and keep expectations in check.

why.true: Correct. That is the reason given.
why.false: Wrong. The text gives exactly this reason.

prompt: True or false: the course text says traditional methodologies suit well-defined, stable projects, while adaptive approaches such as Agile and prototyping suit dynamic environments with evolving requirements.
explanation: That is its conclusion: no single methodology suits all projects.

why.true: Correct. That is the text's conclusion.
why.false: Wrong. The text concludes exactly this.

prompt: Match each methodology with its defining trait.

pairs.right: Each phase completed before the next begins
Subprojects designed, built and tested at the same time
Each development phase paired with a testing phase
Special tools speed up delivery of a portion of the system
Small portions, each adding functionality to the last release
Every iteration is a complete software project

explanation: One trait each. Waterfall is sequential; Parallel runs subprojects together; V pairs build with test; RAD speeds delivery with tools; Incremental adds functionality release by release; Agile makes each iteration a complete project.

prompt: What does the V in the V-Shape Model stand for?
explanation: Verification and validation: testing built in at every development phase.

why.a: Wrong. Not what the V stands for.
why.b: Correct. Verification and validation.
why.c: Wrong. Not what the V stands for.
why.d: Wrong. Not what the V stands for.

prompt: True or false: throwaway prototyping and evolutionary prototyping are the two variants of the Waterfall model.
explanation: Waterfall's two variants are Parallel Development and the V-Model. Throwaway and evolutionary are the two types of PROTOTYPING.

why.true: Wrong. Those are the two types of prototyping.
why.false: Correct. Waterfall's variants are Parallel Development and the V-Model.

prompt: True or false: fourth-generation programming languages and CASE tools are among the RAD tools, and RAD's development cost is lower because the system matches user expectations.
explanation: Both halves hold: 4GLs and CASE tools are RAD tools, and lower cost is one of RAD's advantages.

why.true: Correct. Both are in the text.
why.false: Wrong. Both statements come from the text.
